Title: Overview
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/overview
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# Overview

Review Agent is a self-hosted service that reviews GitHub pull requests on
request. A maintainer comments `/review`; the service reviews the pull request's
current commits with a language model whose tools read the pull request and
record findings in the service's database but cannot write to GitHub, and
publishes advisory findings as pull request comments.

It runs as one deployment per environment: a GitHub App for access, PostgreSQL
for state, and [Hermes](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) as the model
runtime. The model proposes findings. Authorization, the reviewed commits,
stored state, and every GitHub write are handled by code.

| You want to | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Run a first review | [Getting started](./GETTING_STARTED.md) |
| See what a published review looks like | [Example review](../examples/comments/example-review.md) |
| Understand what happens in a review | [How reviews work](./HOW_REVIEWS_WORK.md) |
| Deploy, upgrade, or roll back | [Deployment](./DEPLOYMENT.md) |
| Register, approve, or share the GitHub App | [GitHub App setup](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md) |
| Hand the setup to a coding agent | [AI-assisted setup](./AI_ASSISTED_SETUP.md) |
| Give a repository its own instructions and decisions | [Repository context](./REPOSITORY_CONTEXT.md) |
| Answer findings and record design decisions | [Feedback and decisions](./FEEDBACK_AND_DECISIONS.md) |
| Check documentation against code changes | [Documentation review](./DOCUMENTATION_REVIEW.md) |
| Change the reviewer's voice or rules | [Behavior ownership](./BEHAVIOR_OWNERSHIP.md) |
| Add related-code lookups | [Code graph](./CODE_GRAPH.md) |
| Manage teams, access, model connections, sign-in, and usage | [Admin panel](./ADMIN_PANEL.md) |
| See what a team can do and which model account it uses | [Team access and model accounts](./TEAM_ACCESS_AND_MODEL_ACCOUNTS.md) |
| Operate and recover the service | [Operations](./OPERATIONS.md) |
| Assess the trust model | [Security](./SECURITY.md) |
| See what is and is not supported | [Capabilities](./ROADMAP.md) |
| Find a short answer | [FAQ](./FAQ.md) |
| Change the code | [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/CCimen/review-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) |

Title: Getting started
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/getting-started
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-19

# Getting started

Review Agent is deployed once per environment and serves every repository its
GitHub App installations cover. A repository needs no workflow, secret, or
local configuration.

> [!TIP]
> If Review Agent already serves your repository, go straight to
> [Request a review](#4-request-a-review).

## 1. Register the GitHub App

Register the App and store its numeric ID, webhook secret, and private key, as
described in [GitHub App setup](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md#1-register-the-app)
steps 1 and 2. The services read all three when they start.

## 2. Deploy

Follow the [deployment guide](./DEPLOYMENT.md) for Compose, Dokploy, Coolify,
Portainer, or Kubernetes (Helm).

## 3. Install and approve the App

Install the App on all repositories or only selected ones, then approve the
installation in Review Agent. Approval has two modes
([GitHub App setup, step 4](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md#4-approve-the-installation)):

- **Automatic** (the default of `github-app approve`): the first signed
  `/review` or feedback command from a permitted user enables a repository. A
  command from anyone else leaves it disabled, except on 0.5.0-rc.1 and
  earlier.
- **Explicit**: an operator enables each repository with `github-app onboard`
  or **Add repository** in the console.

## 4. Request a review

In an open pull request whose branch is in the same repository, add a new
top-level comment:

```text
/review
```

You need GitHub `write` or `admin` permission on the repository, or a requester
grant in the console
([who can request a review](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md#who-can-request-a-review)).

The review links the head commit it reviewed and lists coverage and findings.
To review a fix, push it and comment `/review` again. If no comment appears,
follow the [runbook](./OPERATIONS.md#runbook).

## 5. Add repository context (optional)

A `.review-agent/` package in the repository gives the reviewer team
instructions, platform context, and accepted design decisions.
[Repository context](./REPOSITORY_CONTEXT.md#start-with-the-copyable-package)
has the copy and validate commands.

## Serve many repositories

One approved installation can serve every repository the App can reach, once
each is enabled ([step 3](#3-install-and-approve-the-app)). All
repositories share one queue and one database, and reviews of one repository
run one at a time;
[add review workers](./DEPLOYMENT.md#scale-and-operate-the-queue) when waits
grow.

Next: [How reviews work](./HOW_REVIEWS_WORK.md).

---

Title: Deploy Review Agent
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/deployment
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-18

# Deploy Review Agent

## Runtime shape

![Compose topology: only admission and the optional console sit behind the reverse proxy. The private GitHub gateway and the optional console hold the App key, Hermes calls the model provider for review inference, and every service shown uses PostgreSQL on an internal network.](../website/static/img/compose-topology.svg)

- One box is a worker type, not a replica; scale review workers and publishers
  independently.
- Expose only admission (`8644`) and, if used, the
  [admin panel](ADMIN_PANEL.md) (`8090`, a separate image). Keep the gateway,
  Hermes (`8642`), and PostgreSQL off the shared proxy network.
- Only the gateway and the admin panel hold the App key; the admin panel uses
  it to read App and installation status and to verify repositories. Hermes and the publisher never
  receive the key or installation tokens.
- Two one-shot jobs, `review-profile-install` and `review-db-migrate`, prepare
  the start; no service that uses the database starts before the migration.
- Optional add-ons: provider control shares Hermes' network, and the code graph
  reaches GitHub and its embedding provider only through the gateway.

## Create the credentials

### GitHub App

Register the App as described in
[Set up and share the GitHub App](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md). Store the App ID,
webhook secret, and private-key file in the deployment secret manager.

### Service secrets

Set `REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET` to the webhook secret entered when
the App was registered; GitHub and admission must hold the same value.
Generate a different random value for the private Hermes API:

```bash
openssl rand -hex 32  # API_SERVER_KEY
```

Generate two more values for PostgreSQL: one migration-owner password and one
runtime password. The live services receive only the runtime login. Do not
reuse a webhook secret as a GitHub token or database password.

## Choose an image

For local development, keep `REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE=review-agent:local` and start
Compose with `--build`. A qualified release supplies two images for
`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`:

| Image | Contents | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `review-agent` | Hermes and the Review Agent runtime | Initialization jobs, admission, gateway, workers, and publisher |
| `review-agent-admin` | Admin API and compiled browser application | Optional operator console |

Both images come from one source commit and release version. Their image
digests differ. The admin image serves the frontend and API together; it has
no Node.js runtime. Keep the source checkout, Compose files, and migration image
on the same release as the services.

Wait for **Publish container image** to succeed, then use the manifest
references from that release's `IMAGE-DIGESTS.txt`:

```bash
export REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE='ghcr.io/ccimen/review-agent@sha256:<release-manifest-digest>'
docker compose pull
```

Set `REVIEW_AGENT_ADMIN_IMAGE` to the admin manifest reference from that same
file when installing the console. Every release publishes only its exact
version tag, after both images pass qualification. Pin digests in production:
a rebuild can change image contents without changing source. The registry
cannot update two tags atomically, so a single available tag does not show that
the release workflow has completed.

The examples use the upstream `ghcr.io/ccimen/review-agent` package.
Organizations using upstream releases keep these image references with their own
GitHub App, database, hostnames, and secrets. A fork publishes under
`ghcr.io/<owner>/<repository>` and `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repository>-admin`, in
lowercase.

Pin PostgreSQL as well. For a Compose deployment, resolve the selected
PostgreSQL tag once and store the resulting repository digest as `POSTGRES_IMAGE`:

```bash
docker pull postgres:17-alpine
export POSTGRES_IMAGE="$(
  docker image inspect postgres:17-alpine \
    --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
)"
printf 'Review Agent: %s\nPostgreSQL: %s\n' \
  "$REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE" "$POSTGRES_IMAGE"
```

Record all selected image references with the deployment. Do not combine a
PostgreSQL major-version change with a Review Agent upgrade.

## Deploy

Follow the section for your platform:
[Compose or Dokploy](#deploy-with-compose-or-dokploy),
[Coolify or Portainer](#deploy-with-coolify-or-portainer), or
[Kubernetes (Helm)](#deploy-with-kubernetes-helm).

### Deploy with Compose or Dokploy

1. **Fill in the environment.** Copy `.env.example` to the platform secret
   store and replace each `replace-with...` value: the webhook secret,
   `API_SERVER_KEY`, the PostgreSQL password, and both database URLs. Set
   `REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_ID` (the example is `123456`) and
   `REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL`. Tuning variables keep their Compose defaults; see the
   [configuration reference](./OPERATIONS.md#configuration-reference).

   **Database logins.** `REVIEW_AGENT_DATABASE_URL` is the migration owner,
   used only by `review-db-migrate`. `REVIEW_AGENT_RUNTIME_DATABASE_URL` needs
   a different login and password, for the live services. Both must target the
   same host, port, and database; the migration job rejects a shared login or a
   different target. The owner must own the application schema, have
   `CREATEROLE`, and be able to grant `CONNECT`; it does not need superuser.
   The job will not take over an unrelated role with the runtime login's name.

   **Model.** `REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL` is required. Without it, Compose stops with
   "Set REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL to the review model" and admission answers `/ready`
   with `503`. `REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL_PROVIDER` is `openai-codex` (the default) or
   `anthropic`; `REVIEW_AGENT_REASONING_EFFORT` defaults to `xhigh`. Choose a
   model the provider account can use. Settings saved in the console become the
   deployment default, and a team can choose its own
   ([model routing](./TEAM_ACCESS_AND_MODEL_ACCOUNTS.md#model-connections)).

   - **Codex** is the simplest first deployment: Hermes supports a ChatGPT
     device-code login, so no API key is needed. Hermes does not document how
     this counts against a ChatGPT plan's Codex allowance.
   - **Claude**: Hermes documents that Claude OAuth requires Claude Max plus
     extra-usage credits; otherwise use an Anthropic API key.

   Choose the values from Hermes'
   [provider guide](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers)
   and [model catalog](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/reference/model-catalog).
   Keep provider API keys
   ([settings](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/reference/environment-variables))
   in Hermes' credential store or Hermes' own `.env`, not in the Review Agent
   `.env`.

   **App private key on Dokploy.** Create a **File Mount** named
   `github-app-private-key.pem`, paste the complete PEM including its `BEGIN`
   and `END` lines, then set:

   ```dotenv
   REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH=../files/github-app-private-key.pem
   ```

   Do not paste the PEM into the environment. Compose mounts the file read-only
   into the gateway and stops before creating it if the file is missing.
   Anyone with Dokploy project access can read file mounts. Rotate the key if
   it has appeared in a terminal, log, screenshot, ticket, or model
   conversation.
2. Create the external ingress network. Dokploy already provides
   `dokploy-network`; a plain Docker host can create its configured name:

   ```bash
   docker network create "${REVIEW_AGENT_INGRESS_NETWORK:-dokploy-network}"
   ```

3. Validate the stack, then choose one start path:

   ```bash
   docker compose config --quiet
   ```

   Local source:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

   Released image after `REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE` is set:

   ```bash
   docker compose pull
   docker compose up -d --no-build
   ```

   `--no-build` prevents a missing pull from being replaced by a locally tagged
   working-tree build.

   Confirm the services started:

   ```bash
   docker compose ps
   ```

   In Dokploy, use **Deploy** after a source commit changes so the platform
   fetches the new revision. **Redeploy** can reuse the existing source
   checkout. Confirm the deployment shows the intended commit before testing.

   Dokploy's default Compose command includes `--build`. For a released digest,
   open **Advanced > Run Command**, copy the displayed default command, and
   replace `--build` with `--no-build --pull always`. Keep Dokploy's existing
   project name, Compose path, and `--remove-orphans` flag. Dokploy prefixes the
   field with `docker`, so the saved command begins with `compose`. This keeps a
   checkout from being built and tagged over the recorded release image.

> [!WARNING]
> **Keep private services off the proxy.** Do not route `hermes-review`,
> `review-worker`, `review-publisher`, `review-github-gateway`, or
> `review-postgres`. Admission and the optional authenticated admin panel are
> the only services on the ingress network.

4. Route the review hostname to `review-admission:8644`.

   In Dokploy **Advanced > Networks**:

   - Detach every service except `review-admission` and an explicitly enabled
     `review-admin` from `dokploy-network`.
   - Leave **Enable Isolated Deployment** off; Dokploy deprecated that option,
     and `compose.yaml` already declares the networks.
   - Keep outbound access on `review-egress` (Hermes to the model provider) and
     `review-github-egress` (the gateway to GitHub). `review-database`,
     `review-runtime` and `review-github-control` are internal and have no
     outbound access.
5. Connect the selected provider and restart Hermes:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec hermes-review hermes model
   docker compose exec hermes-review /opt/review-agent-bootstrap/install.sh
   docker compose restart hermes-review
   curl -fsS https://review.example.org/ready
   ```

   `hermes model` is Hermes' provider setup wizard for OAuth and API-key
   logins. The installer command restores the deployment-selected
   provider, model, and effort after the wizard stores credentials. Credentials
   live in `hermes_review_data`; normal redeploys retain them. Repeat setup only
   after replacing that volume or when Hermes reports an authorization failure.

Dokploy reads `compose.yaml` as a Compose application. Add one HTTPS domain to
admission and keep the generated Traefik settings. The checked-in health checks
cover admission, the private gateway, Hermes, and PostgreSQL.

Use the matching container for operator commands:

| Task | Container |
| --- | --- |
| Connect the model provider, run `doctor`, or run `smoke-test` | `hermes-review` |
| Onboard, disable, or reconcile repositories | `review-github-gateway` |
| Inspect review execution | `review-github-app-worker`, `review-worker`, and `review-publisher` logs |

The profile installer and database migrator exit with status `0` after a
successful deployment. Do not open a shell in those completed containers.

### Deploy with Coolify or Portainer

Import `compose.yaml` as a Compose stack and enter the required values from
`.env.example` in the platform secret UI. Set `REVIEW_AGENT_INGRESS_NETWORK` to
the external proxy network used by the platform. Point the public proxy at
`review-admission:8644`.

Both platforms run the same containers and health checks. Platform-specific
work stays at the proxy boundary; do not publish Hermes or PostgreSQL ports to
the host.

### Deploy with Kubernetes (Helm)

The chart in `examples/helm/review-agent` deploys the main runtime on a
Kubernetes cluster that provides the rest. It expects an existing PostgreSQL
database, three secrets, an ingress controller, a TLS certificate for the
webhook host, a network plugin that enforces network policies, and a storage
class that can provision the 5 Gi volume Hermes and the review workers share.
With the default `ReadWriteOnce` access mode,
one node must have room for Hermes and every review worker. It uses
fixed resource names, so install one release per namespace.

Create the secrets in the target namespace. Set the webhook variable to the
exact value registered in the GitHub App:

```bash
export REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET='paste-the-registered-value'
kubectl create secret generic review-agent-database \
  --from-literal=REVIEW_AGENT_DATABASE_URL='postgresql://migration-owner:...@host:5432/review_agent' \
  --from-literal=REVIEW_AGENT_RUNTIME_DATABASE_URL='postgresql://review_agent_runtime:...@host:5432/review_agent'
kubectl create secret generic review-agent-hermes \
  --from-literal=API_SERVER_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
kubectl create secret generic review-agent-github-app \
  --from-literal=REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_ID='123456' \
  --from-literal=REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET="$REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET" \
  --from-file=github-app-private-key.pem=./github-app-private-key.pem
```

Write the values to `review-agent-values.yaml`. `tlsSecretName` names a
`kubernetes.io/tls` secret for the host, for example one issued by
cert-manager; leave it out only when the ingress controller already serves a
trusted certificate for that host.

```yaml
image: ghcr.io/ccimen/review-agent@sha256:<release-manifest-digest>
model: <review-model>
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: <ingress-class>
  host: review.example.org
  tlsSecretName: review-agent-tls
```

Deploy in three phases. The script stops at the first failure; fix the cause
and run it again from the top:

```bash
bash -euo pipefail <<'HELM_DEPLOY'
CHART=examples/helm/review-agent
VALUES=review-agent-values.yaml
DEPLOYMENTS="hermes-review review-agent-admission review-agent-github-gateway
  review-agent-github-app-worker review-agent-worker review-agent-publisher"

# 1. Drain: scale every workload to zero, delete the Jobs of an earlier
#    attempt, and wait until no application or initialization pod is left.
helm upgrade --install review-agent "$CHART" -f "$VALUES" \
  --set drained=true --set initialize=false
for deployment in $DEPLOYMENTS; do
  generation="$(kubectl get "deployment/$deployment" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.generation}')"
  kubectl wait "deployment/$deployment" --timeout=5m \
    --for=jsonpath='{.status.observedGeneration}'="$generation"
done
kubectl delete job -l app=review-agent-init --ignore-not-found
for app in $DEPLOYMENTS review-agent-init; do
  pods="$(kubectl get pods -l "app=$app" -o name)"
  if [ -n "$pods" ]; then
    kubectl wait --for=delete $pods --timeout=5m
  fi
done

# 2. Initialize: install the profile and migrate the database.
helm upgrade review-agent "$CHART" -f "$VALUES" \
  --set drained=true --set initialize=true --wait --wait-for-jobs --timeout 10m

# 3. Start the workloads.
helm upgrade review-agent "$CHART" -f "$VALUES" --wait --timeout 10m
HELM_DEPLOY
```

The profile and migration Jobs exist only in phase 2, so they never run beside
the workloads or beside an earlier attempt.

| Fails in | State left behind | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase 1 | Workloads may still be running or stopping | Fix the cause and rerun |
| Phase 2 | Workloads at zero; the failed Jobs remain for inspection with `kubectl logs job/<name>` | Fix the cause and rerun; phase 1 deletes those Jobs first |
| Phase 3 | Initialization is complete; some workloads may be running but not ready | Inspect the pods, fix the cause and rerun |

Phase 1 does not wait for the volume: a storage class that binds on first use
binds it in phase 2, when the profile Job mounts it.

Use `https://review.example.org/webhooks/github-app` as the App webhook URL.
Connect the configured model provider inside Hermes once, then restart that
deployment:

```bash
kubectl exec -it deployment/hermes-review -- hermes model
kubectl exec deployment/hermes-review -- /opt/review-agent-bootstrap/install.sh
kubectl rollout restart deployment/hermes-review
```

Only admission has an Ingress. The chart's network policies allow traffic to
Hermes only from the review worker, and to the gateway only from Hermes, the
review worker, the App delivery worker, and the publisher. Without a network
plugin that enforces them, any pod in the cluster can reach both. Pods run as user `10000`, like the
Compose services; change `podSecurityContext` on clusters that assign users
themselves.

Hermes and the review workers share one volume. With the default
`ReadWriteOnce` access mode the chart keeps them on one node, also when only
Hermes or only a worker is replaced; set `persistence.accessMode: ReadWriteMany`
when the storage class supports it.
The volume holds the model login and is kept when the release is uninstalled.
`examples/helm/review-agent/values.yaml` lists every value.

### Finish the setup

After the services are running, install and approve the App as described in
[Set up and share the GitHub App](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md), then run
`review-agent-admin doctor` in `hermes-review`. On Kubernetes, that guide's
`docker compose exec review-github-gateway` becomes
`kubectl exec deployment/review-agent-github-gateway --`, and
`docker compose exec hermes-review` becomes
`kubectl exec deployment/hermes-review --`.

## Upgrade and roll back production

Before an upgrade, make a tested PostgreSQL backup as described in
[Backup and recovery](./OPERATIONS.md#backup-and-recovery). Record the current
and candidate Review Agent digests and the exact PostgreSQL digest. Keep the
current PostgreSQL image during an application upgrade unless the database has
its own reviewed maintenance plan.

If the admin panel is installed, record both its current and candidate
`REVIEW_AGENT_ADMIN_IMAGE` digests alongside `REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE`. Select both
from one qualified release's `IMAGE-DIGESTS.txt`; their release tag and source
revision must match. Preserve `compose.admin.yaml` in Compose commands, stop
`review-admin` before migration, and start it with the matching worker services.
Follow the [admin service procedure](ADMIN_PANEL.md#add-the-service) for the
overlay, hostname, and post-upgrade version check. The Compose and Dokploy
procedures below cover every installed service, including `review-admin` and
the other overlay services; the Helm chart deploys the main runtime only.

The review worker requires the private GitHub gateway at startup, even when
documentation review is disabled. In Compose, its `REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_GATEWAY_URL`
is `http://review-github-gateway:8646` and it is attached to
`review-github-control`. It uses the existing `API_SERVER_KEY`. Keep this
wiring if you maintain a modified Compose file.

Drain every long-running Review Agent component before running a migration.
This prevents an old process from writing against a schema that changed after
its image was built. When a release changes the installed reviewer, a review
still queued under the previous one fails with `review_contract_changed`; the
release's upgrade notes say when that applies. In that case let the
[queue](./OPERATIONS.md#queue) finish before you stop the services, or request
those reviews again afterwards, as
[Failure codes](./OPERATIONS.md#failure-codes) describes.

### Upgrade with Compose

Set `REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE` and `POSTGRES_IMAGE` to the recorded digest references,
and `REVIEW_AGENT_ADMIN_IMAGE` when the admin panel is installed. When the
deployment uses overlay files, export `COMPOSE_FILE` with every installed file
in order, for example
`COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.admin.yaml:compose.providers.yaml`, so that
every command covers the same services.

Record the capacity the deployment runs with, because the script starts every
service from the Compose configuration and the deployment environment alone:
the replica count of each service (`docker compose ps`), and
`REVIEW_AGENT_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` and `REVIEW_AGENT_ACTIVE_JOB_LIMIT`. A value
passed only on an earlier command line, and a replica count given only with
`--scale`, are not kept. Put the two variables in the deployment environment,
or in saved **Settings** once a revision exists, and the replica counts in an
overlay file named in `COMPOSE_FILE` (`deploy.replicas`). Then run:

```bash
bash -euo pipefail <<'COMPOSE_UPGRADE'
APP_SERVICES="$(docker compose config --services |
  grep -vxE 'review-postgres|review-profile-install|review-db-migrate')"

docker compose pull
docker compose stop $APP_SERVICES

remaining="$(docker compose ps --all --format '{{.Service}} {{.State}}' |
  awk '$1 != "review-postgres" && $2 != "exited" && $2 != "created"')"
if [ -n "$remaining" ]; then
  echo "Not stopped; do not migrate:" >&2
  echo "$remaining" >&2
  exit 1
fi

docker compose run --rm --no-deps review-profile-install </dev/null
docker compose run --rm --no-deps review-db-migrate </dev/null

docker compose up -d --no-deps --no-build --force-recreate \
  --wait --wait-timeout 300 $APP_SERVICES
docker compose exec -T hermes-review review-agent-admin doctor </dev/null
docker compose ps
COMPOSE_UPGRADE
```

The script stops and recreates every service of those files except
`review-postgres` and the two one-shot jobs. It does not migrate unless every
other container of the Compose project has exited; a container that is
running, restarting or paused stops it, as does a failure to list the
containers. This also catches an overlay left out of `COMPOSE_FILE`. PostgreSQL remains available while the application is
stopped. The two one-shot commands must exit with status `0` before new
application containers start. They and the `doctor` call read from
`/dev/null`: the script reaches `bash` on standard input, and a container
command that inherited it would consume the remaining lines, ending the script
early without an error.

The script sees only this Compose project. Stop anything else that uses the
same database first, such as a model runtime
[provisioned separately](./ADMIN_PANEL.md#provision-another-connection), and
upgrade it to the same release.

Afterwards compare the replica counts, the worker concurrency and the active
job limit with the values recorded before the upgrade.

### Upgrade with Dokploy

1. Pause **AutoDeploy** for the maintenance window and take the database backup.
2. Set `REVIEW_AGENT_IMAGE` and `POSTGRES_IMAGE` to exact digest references in
   **Environment**, and `REVIEW_AGENT_ADMIN_IMAGE` to the same release's admin
   digest when the admin panel is installed.
3. In **Advanced > Run Command**, keep the project name, Compose path, and
   `--remove-orphans`, but replace `--build` with
   `--no-build --pull always`. Save the pull-only command.
4. Select **Stop** and wait until every long-running application container is
   stopped, including `review-admin` and the other overlay services when they
   are installed. The two initialization containers may already show
   `Exited (0)`.
5. Select **Deploy**. Confirm the intended source commit and image digest. Do not
   continue if the previous application containers are still running.
6. Verify that `review-profile-install` and `review-db-migrate` exited with
   status `0`, the long-running containers are healthy, `/ready` returns `200`,
   and `review-agent-admin doctor` reports `ready: true` from `hermes-review`.
7. Re-enable **AutoDeploy** only after the deployment receipt is recorded.

Dokploy's stop step may also stop the bundled PostgreSQL container. Its named
volume remains intact, and Compose starts it before the migration job. Do not
delete the Compose service or either named volume during an upgrade.

### Upgrade with Kubernetes (Helm)

Check out the release so the chart matches the image, and set `image` in
`review-agent-values.yaml` to the release manifest digest. Then run the
three-phase script from
[Deploy with Kubernetes (Helm)](#deploy-with-kubernetes-helm) again; the
installation and the upgrade use the same script.

Its wait loop is the migration fence: phase 2 does not start until every old
application pod and every earlier initialization pod is gone. If a phase fails,
the table below the script shows the state it leaves; fix the cause and run the
script again from the top. Afterwards, verify:

```bash
kubectl exec deployment/hermes-review -- review-agent-admin doctor
```

### Upgrade notes

#### 0.4.14 to 0.5.0-rc.1

**Before you switch**

- Use this release's `compose.providers.yaml` and `compose.code-graph.yaml`.
  The 0.4.14 files start services by paths that no longer exist:
  `review-provider-control` and `review-code-graph` fail to start, and the
  console, which waits for `review-provider-control`, does not start either.
  The 0.4.14 `compose.yaml` works unchanged. The 0.4.14 `compose.admin.yaml`
  works with a pulled image; to build the console from source, use this
  release's file, which builds from `console/Dockerfile`.
- Let the queue finish first, or request queued reviews again afterwards. This
  release changes the installed reviewer, so reviews queued under 0.4.14 fail
  with `review_contract_changed`.
- Migration 039 adds two constraints: a finding decision must name the
  occurrence it judged, and a changed file's part must be a part of its review.
  If existing rows violate either, the migration fails and changes nothing.

**What moved**

The Python package is `review_agent`, in `src/review_agent/`, grouped into
packages by what they do. Both images install it instead of copying its files,
so the main image no longer holds `/opt/review-agent-bootstrap/plugins/` or
`/usr/local/bin/review_agent_*.py`. Unchanged: installed command names
(`review-agent-*` in `/usr/local/bin`, and
`/opt/review-agent-bootstrap/install.sh`), HTTP routes, table names,
environment variables, reviewer tool names, and the Hermes plugin
`review-agent-tools` in `plugins/review_agent_tools`. Every command that names
a path or a module:

| Where | 0.4.14 | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `review-provider-control` entrypoint in `compose.providers.yaml` | `python -m review_agent_tools.provider_gateway` | `python -m review_agent.hermes.provider_gateway` |
| `review-code-graph` entrypoint in `compose.code-graph.yaml` | `/opt/hermes/.venv/bin/python /usr/local/bin/review_agent_code_graph.py` | `/usr/local/bin/review-agent-code-graph` |
| Console image command | `uvicorn review_agent_tools.admin_api:app_from_environment` | `uvicorn review_agent.console.app:app_from_environment` |
| First platform owner, run in the console container | `python -m review_agent_tools.admin_auth` | `python -m review_agent.console.auth` |
| Operator commands in a source checkout | `python tools/review_agent_admin.py` | `.venv/bin/review-agent-admin`, after `pip install --constraint requirements/requirements-admin.txt -e .` into that environment |

- The console image starts the new command itself; change it only if you
  override the image command.
- This release's `compose.providers.yaml` no longer sets
  `PYTHONPATH=/opt/review-agent-bootstrap/plugins`. Keeping it is harmless:
  the directory no longer exists, and Python skips it.
- The console image's build metadata moved from
  `/app/bootstrap/plugins/review_agent_tools/_build.json` to `_build.json` in
  the installed package
  (`/opt/admin-venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/review_agent/`).

**Source checkouts only.** `admin/` is now `console/`, `bootstrap/profiles/`
is `profiles/`, and the rest of `bootstrap/` (installer, managed
`config.yaml`, Hermes patches) is `hermes/`. Paths inside the images, the image
name `review-agent-admin`, and the service `review-admin` are unchanged.

- A custom profile goes in `profiles/<key>/`.
- The console image builds from `console/Dockerfile`; from the repository
  root: `docker build -f console/Dockerfile -t review-agent-admin:local .`.
- The console API's optional dependency group is `console` (a `main` checkout
  from before this change called it `admin`; no release did).
- After pulling, delete `admin/node_modules/`, `admin/dist/`,
  `admin/dist-preview/` and `admin/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`, which git no longer
  ignores.

**Logs and APIs**

- Logger names follow the module path. Outside `hermes-review`, the prefix
  `review_agent_tools.` is now `review_agent.` (for example
  `review_agent.cli.worker`), and what logged as `__main__` names its module
  (for example `review_agent.cli.github_gateway`). In `hermes-review` the
  prefix stays `hermes_plugins.review_agent_tools.`. The rest of a name
  changed where its module moved;
  [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/CCimen/review-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#where-the-code-lives)
  lists the packages. The two loggers under
  [Review limits](OPERATIONS.md#review-limits) changed (the 0.4.14
  documentation omitted the `hermes_plugins.` prefix):

  | Logger | 0.4.14 | Now |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Diff cache | `hermes_plugins.review_agent_tools.review_diff_cache` | `hermes_plugins.review_agent_tools.review.diff_cache` |
  | Java guidance | `hermes_plugins.review_agent_tools.review_source_tools` | `hermes_plugins.review_agent_tools.tools.source` |

- Console OpenAPI: the schema
  `review_agent_tools__admin_access_api__RepositoryAccess` is now
  `RepositoryAccessItem`, with that `title`, and
  `review_agent_tools__postgres__github_app__RepositoryAccess` is now
  `RepositoryAccess`. Paths and operation IDs are unchanged.
  `FindingDecision.occurrence_id` is now always an integer, never `null`.
- A run's `failure_detail` names `ReviewValidationError` where it named
  `ReviewMemoryError`. Failure codes are unchanged, and details stored before
  the upgrade keep the old name.

**Removed**

- Nine `review-agent-memory` subcommands of the offline learning tools:
  `learning-report`, `coach-export`, `coach-propose`, `coach-verify-proposal`,
  `coach-run`, `coach-record-outcome`, `coach-history`, `validate-replay` and
  `verification-export`. The other subcommands are unchanged.
- From the repository export (`review-agent-memory export`, now schema version
  18): the keys `coach_runs`, `coach_candidates`, `review_verification_runs`,
  `candidate_verifications` and `candidate_reconciliations`. From the
  publications listing: the four `verification_*` fields.
- The tables of the removed tools, with any rows, are retained; this release
  no longer reads or writes them.
- The OpenShift template. The Helm chart under `examples/helm/` remains. An
  installation plan with `deployment.platform: openshift` no longer validates;
  `compose` is the only accepted platform.
- The unused scale benchmark under `benchmarks/` and its page.

Whether the previous release can run against the migrated database is decided
as [Rollback boundary](#rollback-boundary) describes, not by these notes.

### Rollback boundary

The admin API requires every migration shipped with its source revision. Older
console images do not enforce team access and the separate owner and admin
roles, and treat new team members as global viewers. Do not roll back the
console image alone; use a forward fix or coordinated image and database
recovery. Database-ahead readiness alone does not prove that an older image
preserves access policy.

Roll back only to the exact prior Review Agent digest named in the release
record. That record must include the post-migration schema version and a receipt
showing that the prior digest passed `database ready`, `doctor`, and the smoke
test against a restored copy of that schema. If the receipt is absent, use a
forward fix or the verified backup restore instead of an application rollback.

For a verified target, repeat the same drain sequence, select that digest,
rerun the profile installer, and verify database readiness before starting
application replicas. Keep the current PostgreSQL data and exact database image
unless the separate database recovery plan requires a restore.

Never reverse or edit an applied migration. If the previous application cannot
run against the current schema, either deploy a forward fix or restore the
pre-upgrade backup into a separate database and verify it before switching
traffic.

Incompatible schema changes use an expand-first sequence: add
backward-compatible schema, deploy code that accepts both forms, backfill, and
remove the old form only in a later release after every older application
digest has been retired as a rollback target.

## Scale and operate the queue

Each worker process runs up to `REVIEW_AGENT_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` review jobs at
once (`4` by default) and claims work only when a slot is free. PostgreSQL
lets one review run per repository at a time (the part jobs of one split review
may overlap), while priority aging lets older ready jobs advance. Increase the
per-process value while CPU, memory, and provider capacity remain healthy; add
replicas when you need more capacity or failure isolation:

```bash
# In the deployment environment (.env or the platform's secret store):
#   REVIEW_AGENT_ACTIVE_JOB_LIMIT=120
#   REVIEW_AGENT_WORKER_CONCURRENCY=10
# 100 worker slots, and up to 120 reviews queued or running.
docker compose up -d --scale review-worker=10
```

Keep the two variables in the deployment environment, not on one command line,
so that a later `up` or upgrade starts the services with the same values. They
take effect only while no settings revision has been saved in the admin
console. After the first save, change both values in **Settings** and restart
the services that read them
([environment defaults and admin controls](./ADMIN_PANEL.md#environment-defaults-and-admin-controls)).
A replica count given with `--scale` lasts until the service is next recreated
without it; the [upgrade procedure](#upgrade-and-roll-back-production) says how
to keep it.

Worker slots are an upper bound on running jobs, not a count of running
reviews. Each model connection and each team also runs at most four jobs at
once by default, and these workers all serve the shared connection. This
example therefore runs at most four jobs at a time until an owner raises that
connection's **Maximum concurrent reviews** in the console; see
[Limits](./TEAM_ACCESS_AND_MODEL_ACCOUNTS.md#limits).

Set `REVIEW_AGENT_ACTIVE_JOB_LIMIT` at or above the number of active and queued
reviews you intend to accept. The bundled Compose database allows 200
connections; use the pool formula in Operations to size an external database.
Confirm that the model provider accepts the chosen concurrency. Compose limits
each worker container to 64 PIDs. Keep per-replica concurrency at or below 25
for thread headroom, or raise the PID limit after a capacity test.

Scale `review-publisher` the same way when publication wait time grows. The
database prevents two publishers from owning the same delivery generation.

`REVIEW_AGENT_JOB_PRIORITY_AGING_SECONDS` controls how long one priority point
can move a ready job forward. Each idle worker checks the bounded ready queue at
its configured poll interval, so keep the active-job limit near measured
capacity. The queue and job commands are in the
[Operations runbook](./OPERATIONS.md#runbook).

---

Title: Set up and share the GitHub App
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/github-app-pilot
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# Set up and share the GitHub App

Review Agent reaches GitHub only through a GitHub App. The App delivers
`/review` comments to your deployment and issues short-lived, repository-scoped
tokens for source reads and publication.

There are two ways to use it:

| You want to | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Run your own Review Agent | Register your own App, give the deployment its credentials, then install and approve it (steps 1–5). The App can stay private. |
| Let another organization use your deployment | Make your App public and approve their installation ([Share the App](#share-the-app-with-other-organizations)). |

Examples use Compose.

## 1. Register the App

Generate a prefilled registration URL with the release image you will deploy.
Set `--owner` to the account that will own the App and `--owner-type` to
`organization` or `user`. The command needs no network, database or secrets:

```bash
docker run --rm --network none \
  --entrypoint review-agent-admin \
  ghcr.io/ccimen/review-agent:vX.Y.Z \
  github-app registration-url \
  --owner ACCOUNT --owner-type organization \
  --public-url https://review.example.org \
  --homepage-url https://docs.example.org/review-agent/
```

The URL opens GitHub's App registration form with the settings below filled in.
It registers a **private** App: only the owning account can install it.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Homepage URL | The URL supplied with `--homepage-url` |
| Callback URL | Leave blank; Review Agent does not use user OAuth |
| Request user authorization during installation | Off |
| Device Flow | Off |
| Setup URL | Leave blank |
| Webhook | Active |
| Webhook URL | `https://review.example.org/webhooks/github-app` |
| Webhook secret | A new random value used only by this App, for example from `openssl rand -hex 32` |
| SSL verification | On |

Repository permissions:

| Permission | Access | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metadata | Read | Stable repository identity |
| Contents | Read | Source at the reviewed commits |
| Issues | Write | PR comments, reactions, and feedback commands |
| Pull requests | Write | PR state, reviews, and native suggestions |
| Checks | Write | Documentation review checks (optional) |

Subscribe to **Issue comment**, **Pull request**, and **Check run**. Code review
needs only Issue comment; the other two events and the Checks permission serve
[documentation review](./DOCUMENTATION_REVIEW.md). GitHub sends installation
events to every App automatically. No other permission is required.

After creating the App, generate a private key. Record the numeric App ID and
store the downloaded PEM as a protected file. Never commit it or paste it into
a chat.

## 2. Give the deployment the credentials

```dotenv
REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET=<dedicated webhook secret>
REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_ID=<numeric App ID>
REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH=./secrets/github-app-private-key.pem
```

For Dokploy, create a **File Mount** named `github-app-private-key.pem`, paste
the complete PEM including its `BEGIN` and `END` lines, and set:

```dotenv
REVIEW_AGENT_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH=../files/github-app-private-key.pem
```

Compose mounts the key read-only into the private GitHub gateway and, if you
deploy the optional admin panel, into the admin service. The workers, Hermes,
and the public admission service never receive it. Anyone who can read
the Dokploy Compose service may be able to read file-mount content, so limit
project access and rotate the key if it is exposed.

Then start the release as described in [Deployment](./DEPLOYMENT.md).

## 3. Install the App

Open the App's **Install App** page and choose a scope:

- **All repositories**: one approval covers current and future repositories.
- **Only select repositories**: GitHub itself limits which repositories the App
  can reach.

Installing the App does not start reviews. Every new installation is locked
until an operator of the deployment approves it.

Find the installation ID in the installation URL, or list installations:

```bash
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin installations list
```

## 4. Approve the installation

Approval is a Review Agent decision, separate from GitHub's installation scope.
Choose one of two modes per installation.

### Automatic: approve once

```bash
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin github-app approve INSTALLATION_ID \
  --actor "github:OPERATOR" \
  --reason "approved organization-managed reviews"
```

The command re-reads the live installation, requires Contents read, Issues
write, and Pull requests write, and records who approved it and why. It does
not list or enable repositories.

- A repository is enabled when its first signed `/review` or feedback command
  is processed: the gateway requests a token restricted to that repository,
  verifies its identity, checks the sender
  ([who can request a review](#who-can-request-a-review)), and only then
  records the repository as enabled.
- A command from someone who may not send it is rejected with
  `sender_not_authorized` and leaves the repository disabled.
- In explicit mode a comment never enables a repository.

Release 0.5.0-rc.1 and earlier enable the repository before checking the
sender, so on those releases anyone who can comment on a pull request there can
enable it. Use explicit mode on them if that matters.

Platform administrators can do the same in the console under
**Repositories → Access management**.

### Explicit: enable named repositories

Leave the installation in its default explicit mode and enable repositories one
by one:

```bash
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin github-app onboard OWNER/REPOSITORY \
  --actor "github:OPERATOR"
```

The console offers the same action as **Add repository**.

To return an automatic installation to explicit mode:

```bash
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin github-app approve INSTALLATION_ID \
  --mode explicit \
  --actor "github:OPERATOR" \
  --reason "require explicit repository approval"
```

This disables the repositories that were enabled automatically. Repositories
enabled with `onboard` stay enabled.

## 5. Verify

```bash
docker compose exec hermes-review review-agent-admin doctor
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin repositories list
```

`doctor` checks the full App contract: permissions, subscribed events, and the
documentation-review prerequisites. Right after an automatic approval, zero
enabled repositories is normal.

In an open pull request whose branch is in the same repository, post a new
top-level comment:

```text
/review
```

Check that the comment receives a reaction, GitHub shows one successful
`issue_comment` delivery, `repositories list` shows the repository, and one
review is published for the current head commit.

To prove read and publication access without a model call or a GitHub write:

```bash
docker compose exec hermes-review \
  review-agent-admin smoke-test --dry-run \
  --repository OWNER/REPOSITORY --pr PR_NUMBER
```

## Who can request a review

- A user with current GitHub `write` or `admin` permission on the repository.
- A user added under **Repositories → Who can request reviews** in the console.
  Grants follow the stable GitHub account ID and do not change GitHub
  permissions.
- Feedback commands always require `write` or `admin`.
- Pull requests from forks are rejected (`fork_source_not_supported`).
- Comments from bots, edited comments, and comments on plain issues are ignored.

## Share the App with other organizations

One deployment can serve installations from multiple GitHub accounts.
Nothing in Review Agent restricts which account installs the App; the approval
in step 4 is the gate.

**What you do as the operator**

1. Make the App public: App settings → **Advanced** → **Make public**. See
   GitHub's [guide to App visibility](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/registering-a-github-app/making-a-github-app-public-or-private).
   A public App can be installed by anyone who has the link, which is why new
   installations start locked.
2. Send the other organization the install link:
   `https://github.com/apps/<app-slug>/installations/new`. The console shows
   this link under **Repositories → Access management**.
3. When their installation appears in `installations list`, approve it in
   automatic or explicit mode as in step 4.
4. Optionally create a console team for them and assign their repositories, so
   their members see only their own reviews and can use a separate model
   connection. See [Admin console](./ADMIN_PANEL.md).

**What the other organization does**

1. An organization owner installs the App from the link and chooses all or
   selected repositories.
2. Developers with `write` or `admin` permission post `/review` on a pull
   request.

They deploy nothing and hold no credentials.

**What both sides should know before agreeing**

- Their source code and diffs are read by your deployment and sent to the model
  provider configured in your deployment.
- All installations share one PostgreSQL database and one job queue.
- Reviews use the deployment's model route and account. A console team can be
  given its own model connection, and its repositories then use that account
  instead.
- Console teams limit what each member can see. They are an access control
  inside one deployment, not isolation between mutually hostile tenants. An
  organization that needs that isolation should run its own deployment with its
  own App.
- Uninstalling the App stops all access immediately. Review history already
  stored stays in your database until you remove it.

## Change or revoke access

Disable one repository without touching the GitHub installation:

```bash
docker compose exec review-github-gateway \
  review-agent-admin repositories disable REPOSITORY_ID \
  --actor "github:OPERATOR" \
  --reason "pause reviews for this repository"
```

A repository disabled this way stays disabled until an operator enables it
again; automatic activation does not override it.

Suspending or uninstalling the App on GitHub blocks every repository of that
installation. Removing one repository from a selected-repositories installation
blocks that repository. When GitHub access returns, a repository of an
automatic installation is enabled again by the next `/review` or feedback
command from a permitted sender, as described under
[automatic activation](#automatic-approve-once); a repository an operator
disabled stays disabled. In explicit mode, run `github-app onboard` again.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Webhook returns `401` | GitHub and the deployment use different webhook secrets. |
| `installation_approval_failed` | Verify the installation ID, the App key, that the installation is active, and the three required permissions. |
| A new installation cannot review | Expected until an operator approves it. |
| `repository_onboarding_failed` | The installation must be active and include the named repository. |
| `repository_not_authorized` | Approve the installation for automatic activation, or onboard the repository. |
| `sender_not_authorized` | The commenter needs `write` or `admin`, or a requester grant in the console. Feedback needs `write` or `admin`. |
| `fork_source_not_supported` | Use a branch in the base repository. |
| `provider_authorization_denied` | Confirm the App is active and still includes the repository. |

See [Operations](./OPERATIONS.md#runbook) for queue diagnostics and
[Security](./SECURITY.md) for credential and token boundaries.

---

Title: Set up with a coding agent
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/ai-assisted-setup
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# Set up with a coding agent

A coding agent with access to your source and deployment tools can prepare,
deploy, and verify Review Agent. It follows the versioned installation skill,
`skills/install-review-agent/SKILL.md`, from the exact release it checks out.
The Codex and Claude Code copies are included in the repository, so you do not
install the skill yourself. You keep the approvals and secrets listed below.

## Give this assignment to your agent

```text
Set up Review Agent. If an exact source checkout was not provided, read
https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/llms.txt, clone the source repository,
and check out the exact release declared there before doing any setup work.
Follow the repository-local skills/install-review-agent/SKILL.md; its Codex and
Claude Code mirrors are already included in the checkout, so do not install a
floating global copy. Read only the documentation needed for my deployment
platform. Prepare and validate the non-secret installation plan, then show one
concise mutation and rollback plan before external changes. Resolve facts you
can inspect and group missing owner decisions into one request. Never ask me to
paste secrets into chat. Pause only when I must approve the GitHub App,
repository access, secret placement, DNS, model login, deployment, or the first
live /review. Finish with doctor, inventory, dry-run, and one approved
live-review result. Report exact versions and stable IDs. On Dokploy, use Deploy
when the source revision changes and verify the completed deployment commit. If
a team wants repository-specific review guidance, use the versioned
examples/repository-context/.review-agent starter and validate it with
review-agent-admin repository-context validate; never invent or auto-discover
policy files. Mark unknowns as incomplete instead of guessing.
```

Add the target platform, public hostname, GitHub owner, installation scope,
any explicit repositories, and the deployment tools the agent may use. The agent
records the remaining non-secret choices in a validated installation plan.

The assisted path covers Compose-based installations, including Dokploy: the
installation plan accepts only the `compose` platform. For Kubernetes, follow
the manual Helm procedure in [Deploy Review Agent](./DEPLOYMENT.md#deploy-with-kubernetes-helm).

For the optional [admin panel](ADMIN_PANEL.md), ask for it in the assignment.
The agent can prepare the Compose service and hostname from the same release as
the runtime image. You enter the first platform-owner password in the container
terminal; it never goes into the plan.

## Configure only one repository

If Review Agent is already deployed, give a coding agent this shorter assignment:

```text
Configure repository-owned Review Agent guidance for this repository. Do not
change the deployment, GitHub App, installation policy, model, or secrets. Read
https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/llms.txt, check out the exact release it
declares, and use that checkout's skills/install-review-agent/SKILL.md section
"Configure one repository". This mode assumes the target repository is already
covered by an approved Review Agent installation; if it is not, report that
access prerequisite instead of changing the installation. Copy
examples/repository-context/.review-agent only when the target has no
.review-agent/ directory. Otherwise preserve the existing package and edit it
in place. Keep instructions in instructions.md, list technical context
explicitly in config.toml, and store indexed ADRs under
.review-agent/decisions/. Do not invent or auto-discover policy files. Prepare
the environment and validate the target repository with the commands that
section gives for the release you checked out. Show the repository diff and
bounded validation receipt for normal review. The new guidance becomes active
only after it is merged and a later pull request reads it from the base commit.
```

This path needs no Dokploy access, model login, database connection, or GitHub
App administration. The repository owner reviews and merges the package like
other project policy. See [Repository context](./REPOSITORY_CONTEXT.md).

## What the agent may do

| The agent can | A human owner must approve or complete |
| --- | --- |
| Validate non-secret decisions | GitHub App creation and installation |
| Generate a prefilled App registration URL | GitHub installation scope and one Review Agent installation approval |
| Prepare Compose or Dokploy changes | Secret placement and model login |
| Run local preflight and live doctor checks | DNS or production deployment approval |
| Approve one installation or onboard an explicit repository | The first real `/review` and feedback test |
| Validate a proposed `.review-agent/` package offline | Approve and merge repository-owned guidance or decisions |

The agent must not classify feedback or change the reviewer profile without
your decision.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Do not paste a private key, webhook secret, database credential, internal API
> key, model credential, or backup credential into chat. Put secrets directly
> in the deployment platform's protected configuration.

## Where you act

1. **Approve the mutation plan.** Before it changes GitHub or your deployment,
   the agent shows one short plan naming the exact image digest or commit, the
   deployment project, services and public route, the App owner, permissions,
   events, installation scope and activation policy, secret names (never
   values), migration, backup, verification and rollback steps, and every
   remaining human action. Approve only the named scope.
2. **Register and install the App.** Open the prefilled registration URL the
   agent generates and submit it, then install the App. GitHub installation
   scope and Review Agent activation are separate decisions:

   | Owner action | Result |
   | --- | --- |
   | Install the App with **All repositories** or **Only select repositories** | GitHub defines where the App may request a token. Reviews remain locked for a new installation. |
   | Run `github-app approve <installation-id>` | The trusted installation activates an exact repository on its first signed `/review` or feedback command. [Automatic activation](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md#automatic-approve-once) says whose command can do that in each release. |
   | Keep explicit mode and run `github-app onboard <owner/repository>` | Only that named repository is verified and enabled, with either GitHub installation scope. |

   [Set up and share the GitHub App](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md) owns the details.
3. **Place the secrets** in the platform's protected configuration and mount
   the App private key as [Deploy Review Agent](./DEPLOYMENT.md) describes.
4. **Log in to the model provider.** For a browser or device login, the agent
   gives you the exact container command and waits until you confirm.
5. **Approve DNS and the production deployment.**
6. **Post the first `/review`** as a new top-level comment on a test pull
   request. The agent's dry run needs a repository that is already enabled. If
   it is, for example after `github-app onboard`, post once the dry run has
   passed. On a fresh automatic installation no repository is enabled yet:
   post the first `/review` when the agent asks, and the agent runs the dry run
   after that review has enabled the repository. Test feedback commands only if
   you want to validate that path.

## What you receive

The agent finishes with a report in the skill's completion format: deployed
release and digest, App and installation IDs, activation policy, doctor, queue,
dry-run and live-run results, backup and rollback state, and any remaining owner
action. It contains no secrets. If any of these is unknown, the setup is
incomplete.

---

Title: How reviews work
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/how-reviews-work
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# How reviews work

The model reads code and proposes findings. Everything else is ordinary code:
who may request a review, which commits are reviewed, what is stored, and what
is written to GitHub.

![Review lifecycle: admission stores the signed delivery; the App worker authorizes it through the private GitHub gateway and queues a job; the review worker starts a Hermes session in which the model reads source and the review tools record findings; the publisher rechecks both commits and posts the review. PostgreSQL holds each handoff. The figure shows a review that fits one job.](../website/static/img/review-lifecycle.svg)

A [large review](#5-large-pull-requests) can split into several jobs. A
feedback command stops at the App worker, which stores valid feedback and
acknowledges the comment through the gateway; no model runs.

## 1. Request and admission

1. Someone posts `/review` as a new top-level comment on a pull request.
2. GitHub sends the event to the admission service, which verifies the webhook
   signature and stores the delivery in PostgreSQL before answering.
3. A background worker checks the delivery through the private GitHub gateway:
   - the repository belongs to an approved installation and is enabled, or the
     installation is approved for automatic activation
     ([GitHub App setup](./GITHUB_APP_PILOT.md));
   - the commenter has current `write` or `admin` permission, or a requester
     grant in the console;
   - the pull request is open and its branch is in the same repository.
4. The run is stored with the pull request's base and head commit, and a job is
   queued.

A rejected request never reaches the model.

## 2. The reviewed snapshot

A review covers exactly one base commit and one head commit. File content is
read at those commits. The tools that read the pull request's files and diffs,
record findings, and deliver the review compare the live pull request with
those commits: if the head or base moved, the run ends as superseded; if the
pull request closed, the run stops. A new `/review` starts a fresh run on the
new commits.

If the repository has a `.review-agent/` package, code reads its instructions,
indexed context files, and accepted design decisions from the base commit and
stores them once per run. The reviewer receives them as untrusted input: they
can focus the review but cannot change tools, authorization, or publication.
See [Repository context](./REPOSITORY_CONTEXT.md).

## 3. What the reviewer can do

A review worker claims the job and sends one request to the model through
Hermes. The model session has only these tools:

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `review_agent_begin` | Start the run; returns the overview, changed-file count, and repository guidance |
| `review_agent_pr_files` | Page through the changed-file list |
| `review_agent_pr_diff` | Read diffs, one path or a batch of paths |
| `review_agent_pr_file` | Read a file at the reviewed base or head commit |
| `review_agent_java_guidance` | Load the Java companion when Java code is in scope |
| `review_agent_related_code` | Query the optional [code graph](./CODE_GRAPH.md) |
| `review_agent_memory_context` | Read findings from earlier reviews of the same paths |
| `review_agent_memory_record` | Record findings for this run |
| `review_agent_part_report` | Read part reports in the final session of a split review |
| `review_agent_deliver` | Freeze the review for publication |

Documentation reviews use four separate tools (`review_agent_docs_begin`,
`_scope`, `_file`, `_deliver`); see [Documentation review](./DOCUMENTATION_REVIEW.md).

The session has no shell, file system, browser, web access, delegation, or
GitHub write tool. It never sees the App private key or an installation token.

## 4. The review

The review procedure is a prompt, shipped in the deployment profile. It asks
the reviewer to work in two passes inside the same session:

1. **Find candidates.** Read the diff and the surrounding code and collect
   plausible problems the pull request introduces: correctness, security,
   reliability, maintainability, and clarity.
2. **Try to disprove them.** Check each candidate against callers, tests,
   guards, and invariants, and drop what does not hold.

Security checks follow guidance adapted from
[Cloudflare's security-audit skill](https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill):
trace untrusted input across real trust boundaries and look for the control
that already prevents the problem. This is source review of one pull request,
not a full security audit.

The two passes are instructions to the model inside one session. Code does not
run a second model and cannot verify the model's reasoning. A failed attempt
can be retried, which starts a new session. What code does enforce on every
recorded finding:

- the finding is on a path changed by the pull request and is marked as
  introduced by the diff;
- it has a valid rule, category, severity, line, and fingerprint;
- confidence is at least 0.85;
- the model's publication score is at least 8 for Critical and High, and at
  least 7 for Medium and Low;
- a finding the team has marked false positive or intentional is suppressed
  while the same code context remains and the decision has not expired;
- two findings with identical path, evidence, impact, and fix text cannot both
  be published, and a finding the reviewer grouped under another as the same
  root cause is not published separately. Code does not recognize one defect
  described in different words; grouping those is the reviewer's task.

### Context and retrieval

By default the reviewer sees only the diff and the files it asks for. Nothing
in Review Agent reranks findings or context.

- Findings appear in a fixed order: severity, then score.
- Earlier findings are fetched by exact path, newest first.
- The optional [code graph](./CODE_GRAPH.md) is a retrieval path. It answers
  structural queries (callers, callees, references, tests) and, when OpenAI
  embeddings are enabled, a combined keyword and embedding search from the
  upstream [code-review-graph](https://github.com/tirth8205/code-review-graph)
  library. Each query returns at most ten locations in the order that library
  ranks them. Review Agent adds no ranking of its own, and the reviewer must
  read the source before using a result.

## 5. Large pull requests

Diffs are paged, so a single large file does not block the review. Code splits
the review when the changed files, not counting any file whose own diff is
larger than the largest part, are together larger than that part
([sizes](./OPERATIONS.md#split-reviews)):

1. Changed files are packed in path order into at most twelve parts, sized from
   the model's context window.
2. Each part runs as its own job and session. A part cannot report while a diff
   assigned to it is unread or only partly read; a diff GitHub cannot provide
   is recorded as unavailable.
3. A final session reads every part report, checks the candidates against the
   code, removes duplicates, and delivers one review. It cannot deliver before
   it has read all reports.

A split review costs the first session that registers the files and splits the
review, one session per part, and the final one, and takes correspondingly
longer. In a split review, a file whose own diff exceeds the largest part, and
files beyond the twelfth part, are assigned to no part; left unread, they are
listed under **Coverage details**. When the other files fit in one part, the
review is not split: its one session pages through the large file as far as it
gets, and a diff it does not finish counts as incomplete coverage.

## 6. Coverage

Code records which diffs the tools actually returned. A path counts as covered
only when its whole diff has been returned. If GitHub's limits or a size guard
prevents that, the review says coverage is incomplete instead of reporting a
clean result. Coverage describes what was read, not how well it was understood.

## 7. Publication

`review_agent_deliver` freezes the review as rows in PostgreSQL. A separate
publisher process writes it to GitHub:

- Before it writes each part of the review, it confirms that the pull request
  is still open with the reviewed base and head commits; otherwise it stops and
  marks the publication stale. A push that lands between that check and the
  write is not seen, and a comment GitHub already accepted stays visible; see
  [failure codes](./OPERATIONS.md#failure-codes).
- Stored findings are rendered into a summary comment, split into continuation
  comments when long.
- Up to twelve small, self-contained fixes are posted as native GitHub
  suggestions, and only when the target lines still match.
- Each written comment carries a marker. If the publisher stops after GitHub
  accepted a write, it finds the existing comment instead of posting a duplicate.

## 8. Re-reviews and feedback

Each finding gets a short reference such as `F2`, stable within the pull
request. A later review re-checks earlier findings and reports each as
resolved, still present, returned, or not checked.

Maintainers with `write` or `admin` permission can answer a finding in a new
comment:

```text
/review false-positive F2 because <what disproves it>
/review intentional F2 ADR-0007 because <why the accepted decision requires it>
/review feedback scope F2 because <why it is outside this PR>
/review feedback missed because <what was missed and where>
```

`false-positive` and `intentional` suppress that finding while the same code
context remains and the decision has not expired (180 days for a comment);
`intentional` also requires the named decision to be accepted in the
repository. The two `feedback` commands record evidence for operators.
No command changes prompts or policy on its own. See
[Feedback and design decisions](./FEEDBACK_AND_DECISIONS.md).

## 9. Durability

Jobs, runs, findings, and publications live in PostgreSQL. Workers and
publishers hold leases with a generation number; a process that loses its lease
cannot write. Both can run in several replicas. An interrupted review does not
continue its model session: its job is claimed again under a new lease and
starts a new session, until the job's attempt budget
(`REVIEW_AGENT_JOB_MAX_ATTEMPTS`) is used up; parts of a split review that
already reported are kept. The final session reads their reports under its
live lease, without rechecking the GitHub snapshot. An interrupted publication continues from its stored parts. See [Operations](./OPERATIONS.md).

## Limits

- Reviews are advisory. They do not block merging.
- No code from the pull request is executed, and no tests are run.
- It is not a dependency or CVE scanner and does not replace CodeQL,
  Dependabot, tests, or type checks.
- It reviews the pull request, not the whole repository.
- Pull requests from forks are not reviewed.
- Code review starts only on `/review`. Only documentation review can run
  automatically.

---

Title: Behavior ownership
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/behavior-ownership
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# Behavior ownership

Most organizations need no profile of their own. One deployment uses the
neutral `default-standard` profile for every approved installation and
repository, and each repository can add its own `.review-agent/` package.

## What you can change, and where

| To change | Edit | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The reviewer's identity, tone, and stance when explaining risk | `SOUL.md` in the deployment profile | Every repository served by the deployment |
| Review rules the model follows: scope, severity, coverage, and how it words findings and suggestions | `workspace/AGENTS.md` in the deployment profile | Every repository served by the deployment |
| The review procedure and tool sequence | `skills/review-agent-pr/SKILL.md` (code) and `skills/review-agent-docs/SKILL.md` (documentation) in the deployment profile | Every repository served by the deployment |
| Repository instructions, ordered technical context, accepted design decisions, documentation mappings | `.review-agent/` in the repository ([Repository context](./REPOSITORY_CONTEXT.md)) | One repository, from the pull request's base commit |
| Provider, model, and reasoning effort | `REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL_PROVIDER`, `REVIEW_AGENT_MODEL`, `REVIEW_AGENT_REASONING_EFFORT`, or the console **Settings**; teams can use separate model connections ([Admin panel](./ADMIN_PANEL.md)) | The deployment, or one team |

The first three rows are instructions to the model. They do not change what
code enforces, which the next section lists.

When a request is admitted, the App worker stores its provider, model, and
reasoning effort with the run, whether or not the console is deployed. A saved
route change applies to new requests only.

## What no configuration can change

Authorization, the model's tool set, the reviewed base and head commits and
their re-checks, persistence, the finding gates, and GitHub publication are
fixed in code and in the managed `hermes/config.yaml`. A profile manifest
cannot name a model, provider, tool, or permission, and repository content
cannot change any of them. Fixed GitHub headings and hidden markers are part of
the protocol, not profile templates. See [How reviews work](./HOW_REVIEWS_WORK.md).

## Create a deployment profile

Create another profile only when an environment needs a different shared
identity or fixed review policy. Profiles are part of the image, so a custom
profile means building your own image from this repository.

1. Copy `profiles/default-standard/` to
   `profiles/<key>/`. The key uses lower-case words separated by
   hyphens.
2. Edit the files. A profile contains:
   - `SOUL.md`;
   - `workspace/AGENTS.md`;
   - `profile.json` with exactly `schema_version` (`1`) and `skills`, a list
     of skill keys without duplicates;
   - `skills/<key>/SKILL.md` for each listed skill;
   - `skills/review-agent-pr/JAVA.md`, the Java companion that the
     `review_agent_java_guidance` tool returns when Java code is in scope.
     Keep it from the copied profile: the installer does not check for it, and
     without it that tool returns an error instead of the guidance.
3. Keep `review-agent-pr` and `review-agent-docs` in `skills`. The installer
   rejects a profile missing either one.
4. Build the image and set `REVIEW_AGENT_PROFILE=<key>`. Compose passes it to
   the services, and the one-shot `review-profile-install` service installs
   the profile into `HERMES_HOME` before the reviewer starts.

The installer checks the profile's structure and that every listed skill
exists. It does not interpret their text. It writes a receipt of the installed
profile and skills, and on the next install it removes skills that the previous
profile installed and the new one does not list. Outside Compose, the installer
reuses the receipt's profile when `REVIEW_AGENT_PROFILE` is not set.

## Changing `SOUL.md` and `AGENTS.md`

A change to `SOUL.md` or `AGENTS.md` affects every repository the deployment
serves, so review it as a policy change. Put stable review rules, including
how the model words a finding, in `AGENTS.md`, and procedure in the skill.
Neither changes the layout of the published comment, which code renders. A team
that wants different wording or focus for its own repository uses
`.review-agent/instructions.md` instead.

`SOUL.md` follows Hermes'
[personality and `SOUL.md`](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/personality)
conventions; see also its
[guide to a custom soul](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/guides/use-soul-with-hermes).

Feedback commands and design decisions are described in
[Feedback and design decisions](./FEEDBACK_AND_DECISIONS.md).

---

Title: Configure reviews in a repository
Canonical URL: https://ccimen.github.io/review-agent/docs/repository-context
Status: current
Last verified: 2026-11-17

# Configure reviews in a repository

A repository can add an optional `.review-agent/` package with review
instructions, technical context, accepted design decisions, and documentation
mappings. It is ordinary version-controlled content; no operator change is
needed. A repository without the package gets the deployment's neutral
baseline.

The deployment still owns the reviewer identity, the evidence and security
contract, tools, the model route, and GitHub publication
([Behavior ownership](./BEHAVIOR_OWNERSHIP.md)). Repository content can focus the
review and its wording; it cannot replace authorization, finding gates,
severity rules, tools, or publication.

> [!TIP]
> **Quick path:**
> [copy or edit and validate the package](#start-with-the-copyable-package),
> then merge it. Changes apply once merged
> ([when changes take effect](#when-changes-take-effect)).

## The package

```text
.review-agent/
├── config.toml           Turns guidance on and lists context files in order
├── instructions.md       Engineering principles, review focus, and response style
├── context/              Technical facts the reviewer cannot infer from one PR
│   ├── platform.md
│   ├── backend.md
│   └── frontend/framework.md
├── decisions.toml        Index of accepted ADRs and the paths they cover
├── decisions/            Typed ADRs
│   └── ADR-0001-example.md
└── documentation.toml    Maps source areas to maintained documents
```

Every file is optional. `documentation.toml` and the decision files work without
`config.toml`.

## Start with the copyable package

A Review Agent checkout runs its commands from a virtual environment that
holds the checkout and its dependencies at their pinned versions. Create it
once, then copy the starter only when the repository has no package. Edit an
existing package in place. Then validate the target repository. These commands
belong to the revision this page describes; in a checkout of a release, use
the commands in that checkout's copy of this page:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --disable-pip-version-check \
  --constraint requirements/requirements-admin.txt -e .
repository_root=/path/to/repository
if [ -e "$repository_root/.review-agent" ]; then
  echo ".review-agent already exists; preserve it and edit it in place."
else
  cp -R examples/repository-context/.review-agent "$repository_root/"
fi
.venv/bin/review-agent-admin repository-context validate \
  "$repository_root"
```

Without a checkout, run the same validator from the release image inside the
target repository:

```bash
docker run --rm --read-only \
  --network none \
  --entrypoint review-agent-admin \
  --mount type=bind,source="$PWD",target=/repo,readonly \
  ghcr.io/ccimen/review-agent:v0.5.0-rc.1 \
  repository-context validate /repo
```

The validator needs no GitHub, PostgreSQL, Hermes, model, or secrets. It checks
`documentation.toml` even when the repository has no guidance or ADR index. Its
JSON receipt contains paths, hashes, area IDs, counts, and status, never file
contents.

## Select context files

`config.toml` is the only index of guidance files:

```toml title=".review-agent/config.toml"
version = 1
enabled = true

context = [
  "context/platform.md",
  "context/backend.md",
  "context/frontend/framework.md",
]
```

Review Agent reads `instructions.md` first, if present, then only the listed
context files, in order. Paths are relative to `.review-agent/`, must be under
`context/`, end in `.md`, and appear once. Nothing is discovered by scanning
directories, inferred from repository names, or fetched from elsewhere.

`enabled = false` keeps the files without applying the instructions or context,
and removing `config.toml` opts out of them. A missing listed file or an invalid package drops all
guidance for that review; the code review still runs.

## Write instructions

`instructions.md` holds repository-wide engineering principles, review focus,
and communication style. There is one instruction file; a separate
`personality.md` is not supported. Write rules that survive ordinary
refactors, for example:

- prefer the existing transaction owner for multi-step writes;
